To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the coefficients in the approximate pricing relation are the excess returns on the factor portfolios; and 2) if the riskless asset is included in the regression, the factor portfolios are the only portfolios that have nonzero coefficients in the regression, and the coefficients are the excess returns.
the factor risk premias in the arbitrage theory of finance can be estimated by regressing the returns on the factors in a factor analysis on the excess returns on a riskless asset.

the factor risk premias in the APT are the coefficients in the approximate pricing relation, and that these coefficients are the risk premias on the mimicking portfolios whenever a riskless security and such mimicking portfolios exist.

the factor risk premias are the coefficients in the linear pricing equation.
the coefficients in the APT are factor risk premia, and the factors themselves are risk premiums.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we show that the coefficients of the factor risk premias are the excess returns of the factor mimicking portfolios, which are the portfolios perfectly correlated with each factor.
the factor risk premias are the coefficients of the linear factor model, which is a special case of the APT.
we have provided a very simple proof of the proposition of Ross that the factor risk premias can be interpreted in the arbitrage-pricing theory.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the factor risk premias can be directly estimated from the factor loadings.
the arbitrage pricing model is a natural extension of the capital asset pricing model.
the factor risk premias in the APT can be interpreted as risk premia on the mimicking portfolios, which are often easier to interpret and estimate.
